notes:
I found good coverage for vv. 1–17 and 27–35. Coverage for vv. 18–26 is thin. I didn't get any pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, ligonier.org, 1517.org or lcms.org, so the Catholic views below come from older Catholic commentaries and translations on studylight and biblehub. Where a tradition is missing, I didn't find it.

## Notes on Exodus 34

**Chapter overview**
- The NET notes split the chapter in three: God makes renewal possible (1–4), reminds the people of his moral standard (5–9), and renews the covenant's promises and commands (10–28). https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Desiring God (John Piper, Baptist): Israel broke the covenant almost before it was finished. If it rested on works or strict justice, Israel would be finished. But to show that the covenant is based on grace, God renews the covenant and uses words which make this gracious foundation clear. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-through-moses
- Matthew Henry: when the covenant was broken, Israel broke it. When it was renewed, God made it. If there be quarrels, we must bear all the blame; if there be peace, God must have all the glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/exodus/34.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Moses broke the first tablets because Israel broke the covenant. After Moses prayed for them and they repented, new tablets were fitting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- Dummelow: the words "which you broke" carry no rebuke. Moses is nowhere blamed for his righteous indignation. He was 'angry and sinned not.' https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-34.html
- Bush: God made both the stone and the writing of the first tablets. Now he supplies only the writing. Mercy is restored, but with a reminder of the sin. The wound is healed, but a scar remains. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary
- Word note: the verb "chisel out" comes from the same root as "graven image." Precept Austin sees a touch of divine irony in that, right after the golden calf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary ; https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Matthew Henry: renewing the tablets was the first sign that God had forgiven them. It matches the first promise of the new covenant, that God will write his law on their hearts (Heb 8:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/exodus/34.htm

**v. 2**
- NET: "be ready" probably means Moses was to prepare himself the way the whole people did in Exod 19:11–15. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Precept Austin: "morning" is said twice for emphasis. The mountaintop is where Moses met God before (Ex 19:20). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik: as at the first giving of the law (Ex 19:12–13), everyone else had to keep away. Moses again stood between a sinful people and God as their go-between. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- Janzen (quoted by Precept Austin): this is much like ch. 19, with people and animals kept off the mountain and God coming down in cloud. The big difference is that this time the people don't see it; only Moses does. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 4**
- Precept Austin: Moses cut the stones without complaint, a picture of prompt obedience. The stones are new, but the covenant is a renewal of the old one, not a new one. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary
- NET (citing B. Jacob): the first time, Moses went up empty-handed and came down to smash the tablets. This time the people watched him carry up blank stones, not knowing if they would come back written on. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the cloud was the Shekinah, the cloud of glory seen elsewhere in Scripture. "Proclaimed His name" means God showed Moses his character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- JFB: a cloud may have been chosen because, although God made much of himself known, there was more veiled from mortal view. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- **Who is speaking:** Some commentaries take Moses as the one who "stood" and "called on" the name. The NET argues God is the subject of every verb in v. 5. Moses took his place, God stood by him, and the phrase means God announced himself by name rather than Moses praying. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: this fulfils God's promise in 33:19–23. Hidden in the rock, Moses saw God's "back," as much glory as he could bear. "Merciful" means full of compassion. "Gracious" means stooping in kindness to give the undeserving what they haven't earned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- Matthew Henry: earlier God made himself known by "I AM," his self-existence. now he makes himself known in the glory of his grace, and goodness, and all-sufficiency to us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/exodus/34.htm
- NET: Cassuto suggests reading "The LORD, the LORD" as "Yahweh, He is Yahweh," echoing "I am that I am." "Slow to anger" literally means "long of anger": his anger holds back to give people time to repent. "Steadfast love" and "faithfulness" may together mean "faithful covenant love." https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Piper: later prophets quote this verse. Joel and Jonah both understood God's forgiveness to depend on people turning back to him. So the assumption is that the people whom the Lord will not forgive are the unrepentant people who will not return to God with all their heart. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-lord-a-god-merciful-and-gracious

**v. 7**
- Guzik: "iniquity, transgression and sin" are listed together so no one thinks some sin is beyond forgiveness. He says the passage rules out a harsh Old Testament God set against a kind New Testament one. God's love doesn't cancel his justice; the work of Jesus satisfies it. "Third and fourth generation" is a common Semitic way of saying "continuing" (citing Cole). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- NET: as in 20:5–6, sin and its punishment carry on in a family if left unchecked. It lasts far less than the blessing (thousands of generations against three or four) and is limited to those who hate God. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Piper: the sins of the fathers are punished in the children through becoming the sins of the children. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-god-visits-sins-on-the-third-and-fourth-generation
- GotQuestions: in context the fathers' sins are idolatry and unbelief, shown when the wilderness generation died before reaching the land. https://www.gotquestions.org/iniquity-of-the-fathers.html
- **Translation difference (Catholic):** The Douay-Rheims, which follows the Latin Vulgate, renders the middle line differently: "no man of himself is innocent before thee." https://biblehub.com/exodus/34-7.htm
- **Debated popular teaching ("generational curses"):** Some deliverance ministries use this verse to teach inherited curses. I found only critics, not the proponents' own pages:
  - TGC Africa says such teachers take the verse out of context. It is not that believers by transference receive curses from their ancestors. God is the one who brings them upon those who disobey him, or hate him, or worship idols. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/video/generational-curses-two-dangerous-consequences/
  - Piper says no one in either Testament is trapped or enslaved or in bondage or under an unbreakable curse because of something the fathers did. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/can-my-life-be-plagued-by-generational-sins-hexes-or-curses
  - A biblehub article says the clause is about earthly consequences, not eternal guilt, and points to Deut 24:16 and Ezek 18. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Exodus_34_7_mention_iniquity.htm

**v. 8**
- Matthew Henry: Moses' quick bow shows humble reverence. Even God's goodness should be met with deep awe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/exodus/34.htm
- Guzik: Moses' first response was worship. If we have no urge to worship God, we don't really appreciate who he is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Moses admits the people are stubborn and asks for grace, not justice. Knowing God is forgiving should lead us to ask him to forgive us, and to pray for others too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- Precept Austin: "Then" in v. 10 links God's reply to this prayer. God answered by renewing the covenant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 10**
- Guzik: this is God's covenant, set by him, not bargained over. God would show his glory to the nations through Israel, either by striking blessing or by striking discipline that still kept them a nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- NET: the word for the wonders being "done" is the Hebrew for "create," a verb used only of God, so these are supernatural acts. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting Currid: "making" a covenant is literally "cutting" one, because shedding blood was so central to making treaties. Kaiser: God was remaking the same Sinai covenant, not just reminding them of it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God promises to do what Israel can't do alone, drive out the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- Precept Austin: a command comes before the promise. This is a conditional covenant, with blessing tied to obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 12**
- NET: a "snare" is a trap or lure that leads to ruin (see 23:33). https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Precept Austin: God has just "cut" a covenant with Israel and now forbids them to "cut" one with idol-worshippers, since that would bind them to idols. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 13**
- Guzik: this repeats 23:24. Canaanite religion was too corrupt to keep any part of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- NET: Asherah was a leading Canaanite fertility goddess, worshipped at groves or at wooden poles. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Biblehub: archaeologists have found Canaanite altars with standing stones and female figurines. https://biblehub.com/exodus/34.htm

**v. 14**
- NET: here the text says "other god," where 20:3 has "gods." The "name" Jealous stresses that this is God's nature. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: Canaanite worship was tied to sexual immorality, with fertility gods and ritual prostitution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- NET: "prostitute themselves" pictures leaving true worship as unfaithfulness in a marriage, which is why God is "jealous." It may also be literal, since immorality really happened at Canaanite shrines. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Precept Austin: Israel was God's "wife," already unfaithful through the calf (Jer 31:32). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 17**
- Guzik: this repeats the second commandment and hits hard after the golden calf. No cast image could show God's glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/

**v. 18**
- Guzik: the feast (Ex 12:14–20) pictured the purity God wanted, with leaven, a symbol of sin, put away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/

**vv. 19–20**
- NET: the phrase is literally "everything that opens the womb." "Empty-handed" is the Hebrew adverb "empty." https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 21**
- NET: "plowing and harvest" may be a merism, two extremes standing for the whole year, so the Sabbath applies even in the busiest season (citing Dahood). https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 22**
- NET: "the turn of the year" means the end of the farming season. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 23**
- NET: "Lord" is placed before God's name perhaps to form a contrast with Baal (which means "lord" as well) and to show the sovereignty of Yahweh. But the distinct designation "the God of Israel" is certainly the point of the renewed covenant relationship. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 24**
- NET: "covet" here means more than wanting. It means acting to take the land. God promises that no one will seize it while the men are away at the feasts. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- NET points back to its note on the same command in 23:19. I didn't find a reading of the "young goat in its mother's milk" rule in what I read. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 27**
- Precept Austin: God stresses "these words" a second time (after v. 10). The covenant is "with you and with Israel," meaning with Moses and with the people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 28 – Who wrote on the tablets?**
- **God wrote them.** JFB says the Ten Commandments on the new tablets were written by God Himself (compare Deu 10:1-4). Bush also says the writing was God's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_034.cfm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary
- **Moses wrote them, as God's agent.** NET: in the end Moses wrote, and this is no contradiction, since God is often credited with what he has people do for him. Kaiser: what Moses said, God said. Precept Austin links this to inspiration (2 Pet 1:21). https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary
- JFB: Moses fasted forty days as before (24:18), kept alive for his special task. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- NET: "Ten Commandments" is literally "the ten words." https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm

**v. 29 – The shining face**
- Guzik: the glow was reflected, received glory, not Moses' own. He didn't know because he was humble. Spurgeon: Moses' face shone because he had looked so long on God's face. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- JFB: the glow showed where he had been and marked him as God's ambassador. He carried his credentials on his face. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- Matthew Henry: some people truly reflect God's grace without knowing it. Their friends see much of God in them, but they themselves are ready to think they have no grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- Clarke (Methodist): Moses' body as well as his soul was filled with God's glory. He compares it to Moses at the Transfiguration. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/exodus/34-29.html
- Trench (quoted in JFB Unabridged): this was a weaker transfiguration, a faint preview of Christ's glory shining from within. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/exodus-34.html
- Calvin (Reformed): the word comes from "horn," and therefore it is probable that rays shone forth from his face, which rendered it luminous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/34-29.html
- **"Horns" (Catholic translation history):**
  - Jerome's Latin Vulgate used *cornuta*, "horned." That led artists, Michelangelo included, to give Moses horns. GotQuestions thinks Jerome probably meant "horns of light." https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-horns.html
  - The Douay-Rheims, translated from the Vulgate, keeps "horned." https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-horns.html
  - The Catholic Church's modern revised Latin (Nova Vulgata, 1979) now says the skin of his face "shone" (*resplenderet*). https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/jvl/exodus/34-29.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** the word comes from the noun for a "ray of light" (Hab 3:4). Some have defended "horns," even suggesting a horned mask, but the subject of the verb is the skin of his face (Cassuto). NET also advises reading the story in its own setting before bringing in Paul. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- The Greek Old Testament says his face "has been glorified," linking it to the glory that later filled the tabernacle. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Moses_face_shine_in_Exodus_34_33.htm

**v. 30**
- Matthew Henry: even so, they later grumbled against him, for the most sensible proofs will not of themselves conquer an obstinate infidelity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- Biblehub: their fear shows God's holiness and that sinful people can't freely approach him. https://biblehub.com/exodus/34-33.htm

**vv. 31–32**
- NET: these verses show God's glory confirming the message. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Precept Austin: the glow confirmed Moses as leader and go-between, confirmed God's presence and showed his greatness. What pagan worshiper ever glowed with the reflection of an idol's glory? https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-34-commentary

**v. 33 – When did Moses put on the veil?**
- **While speaking (the KJV's "till").** Gill says Moses veiled as soon as he saw the glow and kept it on while he spoke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-33.htm
- **After speaking.** Ellicott says the KJV exactly inverts the meaning, which is that "when Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face." The Pulpit Commentary agrees, citing the Targums. Moses gave God's message with his face uncovered, then wore the veil the rest of the time. https://biblehub.com/exodus/34-33.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-33.htm
- The Catholic Haydock commentary says Protestants put "till" in italics to suggest Moses spoke veiled. It favours Calmet's reading that he veiled himself after addressing the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/34-33.html
- Guzik (citing 2 Cor 3:13): Moses wore the veil to hide the fading of the glory, not the glow itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-34/
- GotQuestions disagrees with stressing the fading. It says Paul adds no new facts, and Moses veiled because his face frightened people. https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-veil.html
- J. Vaughan (Biblical Illustrator) says the veil was not out of kindness but judicial, the consequence of sin. https://biblehub.com/sermons/exodus/34-35.htm
- Benson (Methodist): the veil stood for the dimness of the old system, which held much of Christ hidden from view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-33.htm
- Matthew Henry draws a lesson of modesty and humility. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_034.cfm

**v. 34**
- Cambridge Bible (on biblehub): the verbs describe what Moses did regularly. NET agrees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-34.htm ; https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/exo34_notes.htm
- Benson: every veil must be laid aside before the Lord. Gill links this to conversion, when the veil of unbelief is lifted (2 Cor 3:16). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-34.htm
- JFB: it was right to remove it before God, since everyone is uncovered to the all-seeing God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_034.cfm
- Biblehub: the glory was renewed each time Moses went back to God, showing that real radiance comes from staying close to him (John 15:5). https://biblehub.com/exodus/34-33.htm

**v. 35**
- Keil and Delitzsch: the glow showed Moses' close relationship with God and the glory of his office. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-35.htm
- How long did it last? Gill reports a Jewish view (Saadiah Gaon, apparently backed by Aben Ezra) that it stayed until Moses died, linking it to Deut 34:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/34-35.htm GotQuestions assumes it faded once Moses stopped going regularly into God's presence. https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-veil.html
- Paul's use in 2 Cor 3 (bible.org): In Exodus chapter 34 Moses, not the people, wore the veil. In 2 Corinthians, Paul changes the imagery, saying that the real veil which obscured the glory of God from the Israelites was their own hardness of heart. https://bible.org/seriespage/30-new-beginning-exodus-3410-35
- Matthew Henry: Moses' shining face was a great honour, yet nothing next to Christ, whose face and whole body shone at the Transfiguration. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_034.cfm

**Gaps**
- I found no distinct Pentecostal, Lutheran or Anglican readings, and no Orthodox material.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The only popular teaching I found is the generational-curse debate on v. 7, and only from its critics.
- The Precept Austin page cut off after v. 2, so its notes on later verses come only from search snippets.
